result.question: How should a portable Linux network appliance (an edge router + Wi-Fi access point using a Broadcom brcmfmac FullMAC radio, e.g. Raspberry Pi CM5/Pi4 BCM43455) automatically determine and apply the correct Wi-Fi regulatory domain (ISO 3166 country code) from its WAN exit / public IP address — reliably, privacy-respectingly, and in regulatory compliance — then bring up the AP (hostapd SSID) on that regdomain? Research and compare concretely: (1) GeoIP methods to map the WAN public IP → country: free/low-friction online APIs (e.g. ip-api.com, ipinfo.io, ifconfig.co, Cloudflare trace, RIPEstat) vs OFFLINE embeddable databases (MaxMind GeoLite2 Country, DB-IP, IP2Location LITE) — for each give accuracy, licensing (can it ship in an Apache-2.0 appliance image?), DB size on disk, update cadence, and privacy posture (does it leak the box's identity?). (2) How OpenWRT and commercial routers/APs actually handle Wi-Fi regulatory-domain auto-configuration today (regulatory.db/wireless-regdb, CRDA deprecation, the 'US'/'00' world default problem, any geo-based auto-set). (3) The 802.11d 'country IE' / passive-scan-to-learn-country approach and why it's insufficient/unsafe to rely on alone for an AP. (4) The correct order of operations to APPLY the domain before hostapd starts (iw reg set + hostapd country_code + ieee80211d), and the known brcmfmac constraint that a RUNTIME 'iw reg set' while hostapd is running triggers a DFS channel-bounce (collapses an 80MHz AP to a 20MHz DFS channel) — so it must be set at boot before the radio comes up. (5) A robust FALLBACK ORDER when the box is air-gapped or geoIP is unavailable and there is no cellular modem: operator-declared country (intent) > cached last-known-good > cellular MCC > WAN-IP geoIP (opt-in) > system timezone → country > world '00' — and how to make each step fail SAFE (never leave hostapd with an invalid 'auto', and prefer the more restrictive domain when uncertain). (6) The legal/compliance dimension: is it lawful/advisable to transmit on a GEO-DETECTED domain vs an operator-DECLARED one, and what the FCC/ETSI/portable-device norms say about a device that moves between countries. Deliverable: a concrete, ranked recommendation for what THIS appliance should implement (which geoIP source, online-with-offline-fallback or offline-only, the exact apply-at-boot sequence, and the fallback ladder), with citations.
result.summary: For this portable brcmfmac-based edge AP, the appliance should NOT geo-auto-set as its primary path: operator-declared country (intent) must be the authoritative, legally-accountable source of the Wi-Fi regulatory domain, with WAN-IP GeoIP used only as an advisory/validation hint — exactly the model Cisco Meraki ships (GeoIP compared against an operator-declared network country, mismatches raise alerts, and a manual override requires accepting legal responsibility). For the GeoIP hint, embed an OFFLINE country-level database rather than call an online API (which leaks the box's identity and fails when air-gapped); the single license-clean choice for an Apache-2.0 image is sapics/ip-location-db 'user-country' (ODC-PDDL, no attribution, no share-alike, ~8MB, ~97.5% country-agreement with GeoLite2) — MaxMind GeoLite2 needs a paid commercial-redistribution license, and DB-IP Lite (CC BY 4.0) / IP2Location LITE and IPLocate (both CC BY-SA 4.0 share-alike) carry attribution or copyleft obligations. Apply the domain at BOOT before the radio comes up (write regulatory.db country via `iw reg set` + set hostapd `country_code` + `ieee80211d=1` before hostapd starts), because a runtime `iw reg set` on brcmfmac while hostapd runs triggers a DFS channel-bounce that collapses an 80MHz AP to 20MHz. Use a fail-safe fallback ladder — operator-declared > cached last-known-good > cellular MCC > WAN-IP GeoIP (opt-in) > timezone→country > world '00' — where every rung defaults to the restrictive world '00' domain (the kernel's own fail-safe default) rather than an invalid 'auto', preferring the more restrictive domain when uncertain.

findings.claim: For an Apache-2.0 appliance image, the only fully license-clean offline IP-to-country database to embed is sapics/ip-location-db 'user-country' (ODC-PDDL: no attribution, no share-alike); MaxMind GeoLite2 requires a paid per-product Commercial Redistribution License, while DB-IP Lite (CC BY 4.0), IP2Location LITE DB1 (CC BY-SA 4.0), and IPLocate (CC BY-SA 4.0) impose attribution and/or share-alike obligations.
findings.evidence: GeoLite2 EULA does not permit bundling into a sold product ('for every product you sell that incorporates the GeoLite database, you must purchase an additional Commercial Redistribution License'). sapics 'user-country' is published under PDDL v1.0 with 'free use without attribution' and is deliberately engineered PDDL-clean (no RIR WHOIS/IRR). DB-IP Lite = CC BY 4.0 (attribution/link-back required). IP2Location DB1 and IPLocate = CC BY-SA 4.0 (attribution + ShareAlike copyleft — a genuine compatibility concern for an Apache-2.0 image).

findings.claim: The 'user-country' PDDL database is compact enough to embed on an edge appliance and accurate enough for regulatory-domain hinting: country-level free-DB accuracy is 95-99%, and user-country is ~97.5% country-code-identical to GeoLite2 (vs 94.49% for DB-IP Lite, 78.50% for iptoasn); comparable offline country DBs ship at roughly 8MB MMDB.
findings.evidence: June 2026 IPv4 comparison table: user-country 97.49% same / 2.51% diff / 0.00% empty; dbip-country 94.49%; iptoasn-country 78.50% same with 15.66% empty. DB-IP Lite MMDB = 7.8MB compressed (696,624 ranges, accuracy index 81 vs 93 commercial); IPLocate MMDB = 16.1MB (2.1M entries). Country-level geolocation is 95-99% accurate (MaxMind self-reports ~99.8%), while city-level is only 55-80% — so country-only DBs are the right granularity and city detail is unnecessary.

findings.claim: Prefer an offline embedded database over online GeoIP APIs: online lookups (ip-api.com, ipinfo.io, Cloudflare trace, RIPEstat) leak the box's public IP/identity to a third party and fail when air-gapped, whereas an embedded MMDB performs sub-millisecond offline lookups with no external calls.
findings.evidence: IPLocate's own page states the MMDB lets you 'perform ultra-fast, offline lookups without any external API calls.' An offline DB is the privacy-respecting and air-gap-tolerant choice; the appliance already needs the WAN public IP locally, so no outbound request that reveals the device is required. (Note: to map WAN IP→country the box still needs to know its own public/exit IP; when behind CGNAT/VPN the exit IP may resolve to the wrong country, an inherent GeoIP limitation.)

findings.claim: Operator-declared country (intent) should be the authoritative, legally-accountable source of the regulatory domain, with WAN-IP GeoIP used only as an advisory/validation hint — matching how a major commercial vendor (Cisco Meraki) actually ships regulatory auto-config.
findings.evidence: Meraki determines the domain from ship-to location plus Geo-IP at dashboard check-in, but enforcement compares Geo-IP against the operator-defined network country ('the source of truth') and raises ALERTS on mismatch rather than silently trusting GeoIP. A manual override to a declared country requires accepting a legal agreement making the user responsible for compliance and asserting the APs' physical location matches. This validates treating GeoIP as a cross-check, not a silent auto-set, and operator-declaration as the legally-accountable path.

findings.claim: Apply the regulatory domain at BOOT before the radio/hostapd comes up: set the kernel regdomain (iw reg set / regulatory.db country), plus hostapd country_code and ieee80211d=1 — because on brcmfmac a runtime 'iw reg set' while hostapd is running triggers a DFS channel-bounce that collapses an 80MHz AP to a 20MHz DFS channel.
findings.evidence: hostapd.conf documents country_code as a two-char ISO/IEC 3166-1 code that 'Used to set regulatory domain' (limits channels/TX power), and ieee80211d=1 'advertises the country_code and the set of allowed channels and transmit power levels' but 'must be configured with the correct country' to function. Since kernel v4.15 the regdb is loaded in-kernel from /lib/firmware/regulatory.db (CRDA no longer required, commit 007f6c5e6eb45). The brcmfmac DFS-bounce constraint (from project field memory) means the country MUST be committed before the radio initializes; OpenWRT similarly sets per-radio country via UCI and verifies with 'iw reg get' after reboot. Order: set kernel reg domain → hostapd country_code + ieee80211d=1 → start hostapd.

findings.claim: Do NOT rely on 802.11d country-IE / passive-scan-to-learn-country alone for an AP: the country IE is only trusted after intersection with the kernel regdb, is a client-side learn mechanism (not an AP domain source), and a disconnected station in the OTHER domain is restricted to passive scanning.
findings.evidence: cfg80211 builds the applied rules from 'the intersection of data from the APs country information element and what CRDA provides for the given country code' — the IE alone does not define rules (guards against outdated/rogue APs). The passive-learn mechanism enforces a domain only when a domain change is 'detected by observing an AP', which requires another AP already transmitting a country IE — useless as the first-boot source for a device that IS the AP. A disconnected station in DOT11_REG_DOMAIN_OTHER 'must only perform a passive scan on any channel' and may not actively transmit, so an AP cannot bootstrap its own domain this way.

findings.claim: The fallback ladder must fail SAFE to the world '00' domain, never to an invalid 'auto': operator-declared > cached last-known-good > cellular MCC > WAN-IP GeoIP (opt-in) > timezone→country > world '00', preferring the more restrictive domain when uncertain.
findings.evidence: On cfg80211 init the kernel sets the world regulatory domain '00' (highly restrictive) as the central domain by default — i.e. a device with no country set already starts fail-safe/restrictive, which is the correct terminal rung. Because RF regulations differ by country and a device 'needs to obey the regulations for your current location', an uncertain box should choose the more restrictive '00' rather than transmit on an unverified channel/power. Every rung above resolves to a concrete two-char ISO code; if none resolves, hostapd is left on '00' (or refuses to start on DFS/high-power channels) rather than an invalid 'auto'.

findings.claim: Legally/compliance-wise, transmitting on an operator-DECLARED domain is the advisable path for a portable device that moves between countries; geo-detection is a convenience/validation aid, and the operator remains legally responsible for matching the domain to the APs' true physical location.
findings.evidence: Meraki's manual-override path is explicitly gated behind a legal agreement 'specifying the user is responsible for enforcing the right regulatory domain' and that 'the country configured must always match the country where the devices are physically located' — establishing operator-declaration as the legally-accountable norm. OpenWRT's regulation FAQ states the setup 'needs to obey the regulations for your current location.' This is a synthesis of vendor practice + regulatory principle rather than a direct FCC/ETSI citation, hence medium confidence; the underlying facts (regs differ by country, device must obey current location) are 3-0 confirmed.

result.caveats: Direct FCC Part 15 / ETSI EN 300 328 primary-text citations were not captured in the surviving claims — the compliance finding rests on vendor practice (Meraki) plus the OpenWRT secondary FAQ and the general 'regulations differ by country' fact, so the specific legal posture on GEO-detected vs DECLARED domains is medium-confidence and should be reviewed by counsel before shipping a geo-auto-set default. The brcmfmac runtime-'iw reg set' DFS channel-bounce constraint is asserted from project field memory (hookprobe-wifi-brcmfmac-caps), not from an external primary source in the verified set, though it is consistent with the documented boot-order requirement. GeoIP accuracy figures (95-99% country) are point-in-time and drift; the WAN-exit-IP→country mapping is inherently unreliable behind CGNAT, carrier NAT, or a VPN whose tunnel exits in another country (Meraki explicitly documents this failure mode) — which is itself the strongest argument for operator-declared primacy. sapics 'user-country' MMDB packaging may be a community/secondary artifact (upstream distributes CSV); verify an MMDB build exists or generate one at build time. The refuted claim that free DBs are uniformly CC BY-SA 4.0 was wrong — licenses differ per database, so the specific chosen DB's license must be re-checked at each update. DB entry counts and file sizes are monthly-updated snapshots.
openQuestions: What are the exact FCC (47 CFR Part 15) and ETSI EN 300 328 / EN 301 893 provisions governing a PORTABLE device that changes countries — is a geo-detected auto-set domain ever compliant, or must the domain always be operator-attested?
Does a prebuilt MMDB of sapics/ip-location-db 'user-country' exist upstream, or must the appliance build the MMDB from the PDDL CSV at image-build time (and does that derived MMDB remain PDDL-clean)?

How should the box obtain its own WAN public/exit IP for the offline lookup without an external call (e.g. from the WAN interface, PPPoE assignment, or a STUN-like probe) when behind CGNAT — and what is the confidence-downgrade rule when the exit IP is a known VPN/CGNAT range?
What is the precise cellular MCC→ISO-3166 mapping path and priority when a cellular modem is present but the WAN exit (VPN) resolves to a different country than the SIM's serving network?

refuted.claim: The free databases are licensed under CC BY-SA 4.0, which permits commercial redistribution/embedding but requires attribution AND that derivatives be shared under the same share-alike license.

On OpenWRT, when more than one Wi-Fi radio is present at boot, setting the per-device country code (option country in /etc/config/wireless) has no effect: the global regdomain falls back to '98' (DFS-UNSET) and each radio silently runs on its own EEPROM-derived country (e.g. one radio US, the other GB), which cannot be overridden from software.
